A scenario is valid only when a domain stakeholder could understand it without knowing the codebase. If the `bdd` skill is installed, follow it as the authoritative guide; this file is the board's summary and verifier checklist. #### When Gherkin fits Use it for user- or stakeholder-observable behavior: business rules, permissions, state transitions, money, safety, privacy, cross-role workflows, failure and recovery. Don't use it for internal refactors, framework mechanics, or unit-level logic — write behavior-level acceptance criteria or test plans instead, and say why. #### Discovery before writing Run a short example-mapping pass on the board (Matt Wynne's technique): - **Story / capability** (yellow) — the behavior being specified. - **Rules** (blue) — business rules that constrain it. - **Examples** (green) — concrete cases per rule, including at least one negative or boundary case. - **Questions** (red) — unknowns; these become board `question` artifacts, not invented rules. Too many rules means the story should split; too many questions means it isn't ready. #### File shape ```gherkin # serves: obj-2, dec-0007 source: q-2.1, evidence-support-tickets-q3 Feature: Refund a delivered order Customers can request a refund within 30 days of delivery so that they trust buying from us. Background: Given Dana is a signed-in customer And Dana has an order delivered 10 days ago for $40.00 Rule: Refunds are allowed within 30 days of delivery Scenario: Customer requests a refund inside the window When Dana requests a refund for the order Then Dana sees the refund is approved for $40.00 And Dana receives a refund confirmation email Scenario: Customer requests a refund after the window closes Given the order was delivered 31 days ago When Dana requests a refund for the order Then Dana sees the refund is not available And Dana is offered a way to contact support Rule: An order can be refunded only once Scenario Outline: Repeat refund requests are refused Given the order was already refunded When Dana requests a refund for the order Then Dana sees the order "" Examples: | status | message | | in full | has already been refunded | | partially | has a refund in progress | ``` #### Wording rules - **Given** = relevant prior state or business context; **When** = one actor action or domain event; **Then** = an observable outcome. One `When` per scenario. - Use named personas and concrete values (`Dana`, `$40.00`, `31 days`), not `a user`, `valid data`, `some amount`. - Business language only: no functions, classes, endpoints, DB rows, selectors, mocks, or "clicks the button" unless those words are the user's domain. - Declarative, not imperative: "Dana requests a refund", not "Dana clicks Refund, then clicks Confirm". - Scenario titles state the rule outcome ("…is refused"), not "test 3" or "happy path". - Use `Rule:` to group scenarios by business rule; `Background:` only for setup shared by every scenario in the feature and kept to a few lines. - Scenario Outlines only when examples vary data, not behavior. #### Coverage expectations For each rule, consider: happy path; boundary values; invalid input; permission denied; duplicate or repeated action; expired or stale state; unavailable dependency; concurrent action; partial failure and recovery; accessibility-visible feedback; audit or support outcome. Risky workflows (money, safety, allergies, privacy, permissions, destructive, legal, cross-role, irreversible) must not be happy-path-only — include the most important failure, denial, or recovery scenario or record the missing product question. #### Mechanical check Scenario Outlines, `Background:` and multi-step setups make it easy to lose or double the `When`. Before handing over a feature file, count steps per scenario: exactly one `When` (an `And` directly after `When` counts as a second action — split the scenario or move it into `Given`). If Node is available, parse the file with `@cucumber/gherkin` (`npm i @cucumber/gherkin @cucumber/messages`) and walk each scenario counting `When` and `And`-after-`When` steps; a parse error also catches syntax mistakes. Report the result; don't claim a check you didn't run. Also re-read the numbers in every scenario against the rule it illustrates (thresholds, percentages, dates). A scenario whose arithmetic contradicts its own rule is worse than a missing one. #### Verifier checklist - [ ] Header comment names the objectives/decisions served and the source evidence. - [ ] Feature description states the business value. - [ ] Every scenario has exactly one `When` and an observable `Then`. - [ ] No implementation vocabulary; no vague assertions (`works`, `handles errors`, `correct result`). - [ ] Concrete personas and values throughout. - [ ] Each `Rule:` has at least one negative or boundary scenario where it matters. - [ ] Open questions are on the board, not silently assumed. - [ ] Every scenario maps to a row in the validation plan (or is marked documentation-only with reason). - [ ] Each scenario stands alone; no hidden dependency on another scenario's run order. ### Other documentation formats Compact standards for the remaining documents agents produce. Each entry: purpose, minimal template, and verifier checks. #### Contents Engineering: OpenAPI / AsyncAPI contract · ERD and data dictionary · Threat model (STRIDE) · SLOs and runbook · Test strategy / validation plan · Migration plan Business: BPMN / swimlane process · SIPOC · Business case · Risk register · Stakeholder map and RACI/DACI · OKRs · Business Model / Lean Canvas Product and UX: Persona and JTBD · User story map · Customer journey map · Research brief and findings log --- #### OpenAPI / AsyncAPI contract Purpose: the machine-checkable interface contract for sync (OpenAPI 3.1) or event (AsyncAPI 3) interfaces. Template: paths/channels with operation IDs, request/response or message schemas, error model (RFC 9457 problem details recommended), auth scheme, idempotency and pagination rules, versioning policy, examples per operation. Checks: every operation has success and error responses with examples; breaking vs non-breaking change classified; idempotency stated for unsafe operations; schemas reuse components; names match the domain glossary; compatibility plan for existing consumers. #### ERD and data dictionary Purpose: stored data structure, keys, and invariants. Template (Mermaid `erDiagram`) plus a dictionary table: entity, field, type, nullability, constraints, PII class, retention, owner. Checks: cardinalities on every relationship; primary/foreign keys explicit; PII and retention classified; migration/backfill impact noted for changed fields; matches the UML domain model terms. #### Threat model (STRIDE) Purpose: identify and dispose of security threats at trust boundaries. Template: data-flow diagram with trust boundaries (Mermaid flowchart with subgraphs per zone) → table: element / boundary, STRIDE category (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege), threat, likelihood, impact, mitigation, validation check, residual risk owner. Checks: every boundary crossing analyzed; each material threat has mitigation + check or accepted residual risk with a named owner; abuse cases feed Gherkin negative scenarios. #### SLOs and runbook Purpose: define reliability targets and operational response. SLO template: user journey, SLI (good events / valid events), target, window, error budget policy, alert thresholds (burn-rate), dashboard link. Runbook template: symptom → diagnosis steps → mitigation → rollback → escalation → verification, with commands and expected outputs. Checks: SLIs measure user-observable outcomes; each alert links to a runbook; rollback is rehearsed or marked unrehearsed. #### Test strategy / validation plan Purpose: prove every objective/ask. Template: the validation-plan table in planning-outputs.md plus test pyramid split (unit / integration / contract / end-to-end / exploratory / post-release metric), environments, data needs, flake controls. Checks: every ask has a check with a pass condition someone else can run; cheapest method that observes the ask directly; required security and edge cases appear as checks. #### Migration plan Purpose: move data, users, or systems safely. Template: current → target state; phases (expand, migrate, contract); backfill method; dual-write/read strategy; verification queries; cutover gates; rollback per phase; communication. Checks: every phase reversible or explicitly one-way with decider sign-off; data invariants verified before and after; downtime and blast radius bounded. --- #### BPMN / swimlane process Purpose: how work flows across people, teams, and systems. Template: Mermaid flowchart with one `subgraph` per lane (role or system); events (start/end), tasks, gateways (exclusive "?" decisions, parallel forks), handoffs between lanes highlighted. Include the as-is and to-be views when changing a process. Checks: one start, explicit ends; every gateway branch labeled; handoffs and wait states visible; exception paths (rejection, timeout, rework) shown; cycle time or volume annotations where the board measures them. #### SIPOC Purpose: scope a process quickly before detailed mapping. Template: table of Suppliers, Inputs, Process (5–7 high-level steps), Outputs, Customers. Checks: process steps are verbs at one level; every output has a customer; boundaries (start/end trigger) explicit. #### Business case Purpose: decide whether something is worth doing. Template: problem and objective; options (including do nothing); benefits (quantified with assumptions); costs (one-time, recurring); payback / NPV or simple ROI with stated discount rate; risks; sensitivity analysis on the 2–3 most uncertain assumptions; recommendation for the decider. Checks: every number has a source or is labeled an assumption with a range; sensitivity shows which assumption flips the decision; do-nothing option costed; recommendation separated from analysis. #### Risk register Purpose: track risks to objectives. Template: ID, risk statement ("If , then , resulting in "), likelihood (1–5), impact (1–5), score, owner, response (avoid/mitigate/transfer/accept), mitigation actions as plan steps, trigger/early warning, status. Checks: cause-event-impact form; every high risk has an owner and a plan step or an accepted-by authority; triggers are observable. #### Stakeholder map and RACI/DACI Purpose: who decides, who contributes, who must be told. Template: power/interest grid (manage closely / keep satisfied / keep informed / monitor) and a DACI table per decision (Driver, Approver — exactly one, Contributors, Informed) or RACI per activity (exactly one Accountable). Checks: one approver/accountable per item; affected and executing parties not omitted; contributors have a voice, not a vote. #### OKRs Purpose: align objectives with measurable results. Template: Objective (qualitative, inspiring) → 2–4 Key Results (measurable outcomes with baseline and target) → initiatives (plan steps). Checks: KRs measure outcomes not outputs; baselines exist or a step creates them; each initiative maps to a KR. #### Business Model Canvas / Lean Canvas Purpose: frame a new product or business line. Template: the nine (BMC) or nine Lean blocks; each claim tagged `evidence` or `assumption` with the experiment that would test it. Checks: riskiest assumptions identified and turned into investigation steps. --- #### Persona and Jobs-to-be-Done Purpose: ground decisions in real user needs. Template: persona (context, goals, frustrations, evidence sources) or job statement ("When , I want to , so I can ") with hiring/firing criteria. Checks: based on evidence (interviews, data), not invention; labeled provisional when assumption-based. #### User story map Purpose: sequence user-visible capability into releases. Template: backbone of user activities left-to-right; tasks under each; stories stacked by priority; horizontal release lines (walking skeleton first). Checks: first release is a thin end-to-end slice; each story links to a Gherkin feature or acceptance criteria. #### Customer journey map Purpose: expose pain and opportunity across a whole experience. Template: stages × (actions, touchpoints, thoughts/feelings, pain points, opportunities, owning team), current vs future. Checks: grounded in research; pain points prioritized; opportunities become objectives or questions. #### Research brief and findings log Purpose: run investigations rigorously. Brief template: question, why it matters (objective link), hypotheses, method, sources, sample, bound, what result would change the plan. Findings log: finding ID, statement, evidence (source, date, retrieval method), confidence, contradicting evidence, implication. Checks: findings separate observation from interpretation; contradicting evidence recorded; sources dated. ### UML standard UML is a toolbox, not a deliverable. Use the one or two diagram types that answer a live board question, at the level of detail that question needs. Draw in Mermaid unless the repository already uses PlantUML. #### Choosing a diagram | Question on the board | Diagram | Owner (default) | | --- | --- | --- | | What are the domain concepts, their attributes, and relationships? | Class (domain model) | `domain-modeler` | | Who calls whom, in what order, and what happens on failure? | Sequence | `api-integration-designer` | | What states can this thing be in, and what moves it between them? | State machine | `domain-modeler`, `ux-flow-designer` | | How does a workflow branch, loop, and run in parallel? | Activity | `business-process-analyst`, `ux-flow-designer` | | Which actors pursue which goals with the system? | Use case | `requirements-analyst` | | How are deployable parts wired? | Prefer C4 deployment over UML deployment | `sre-reliability` | #### Class diagram (domain model) Conceptual, not code: names come from the ubiquitous language; include only attributes and operations that carry business rules. Show multiplicities and aggregate boundaries. ```mermaid --- title: Refunds domain model (serves obj-2) --- classDiagram class Order { +OrderId id +Money total +Date deliveredOn +isRefundable(today) bool } class Refund { +RefundId id +Money amount +RefundStatus status } class Customer Customer "1" --> "*" Order : places Order "1" --> "0..1" Refund : may have note for Order "Invariant: refundable only within 30 days of deliveredOn" ``` Checklist: names match the glossary and Gherkin; every association has multiplicity; invariants are noted next to the class that enforces them; no persistence or framework types (`DTO`, `Repository`, `id: int8`) unless the diagram is explicitly a design-level class diagram. #### Sequence diagram Show one scenario per diagram, including the failure branch that matters. Name participants by role or container (consistent with C4), not by class. ```mermaid --- title: Refund request — happy path and payment-provider timeout (serves dec-0007) --- sequenceDiagram actor Dana as Customer participant Web as Web app participant API as Orders API participant Pay as Payment provider Dana->>Web: Request refund Web->>API: POST refund(orderId) API->>API: check 30-day rule alt within window API->>Pay: refund($40.00, idempotency key) alt provider responds Pay-->>API: refunded API-->>Web: approved else timeout after 5s API-->>Web: pending, will retry Note over API,Pay: retry with same idempotency key end else outside window API-->>Web: not refundable end ``` Checklist: one scenario per diagram; failure/timeout branch included where the board flagged it; idempotency, retries, and timeouts explicit for remote calls; participants match C4 container names; messages are business-meaningful. #### State machine Use when the board has lifecycle rules ("can a cancelled order be refunded?"). ```mermaid --- title: Refund lifecycle --- stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Requested Requested --> Approved: within window Requested --> Rejected: outside window Approved --> Paid: provider confirms Approved --> Pending: provider timeout Pending --> Paid: retry succeeds Pending --> Failed: retries exhausted Paid --> [*] Rejected --> [*] Failed --> Requested: support re-opens ``` Checklist: every state reachable and every non-final state has an exit; guards written as business conditions; terminal states explicit; each transition that users can observe has a Gherkin scenario; illegal transitions listed if the board asked about them. #### Activity diagram Use Mermaid `flowchart` for activity flows when swimlanes are not essential; use BPMN (see other-formats.md) when handoffs between people or departments are the point. Checklist: one start, explicit ends; decisions labeled with conditions on every branch; parallel work shown as fork/join; loops have an exit condition. #### Use case diagram Mermaid has no native use-case diagram; use a flowchart with actors as stadium shapes and use cases as rounded boxes, or a use-case table: | Actor | Goal (use case) | Trigger | Main success outcome | Key extensions | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | Checklist: goals are user goals, not UI steps; each use case links to a Gherkin feature or is marked out of scope. #### Common mistakes - Reverse-engineering every class from code into one giant diagram — answer a question instead. - Mixing conceptual and implementation levels in one view. - Sequence diagrams with only the happy path when the board's risk is the failure path. - State diagrams missing the "stuck" states (pending, failed, expired). ### Planning outputs The plan is the deliverable the user acts on. Project it from the board: every step is a `plan-step` artifact that traces to objectives, questions or asks, decisions, and documents. Pick the template for the mode; chained modes produce one section per mode. #### Contents - Step fields - Investigation plan - Decision plan - Implementation plan - Rendering rules - Worked mini-example #### Step fields | Field | What good looks like | Weak version to rewrite | | --- | --- | --- | | `id` | `S3` or `inv-3`, stable across revisions | — | | objective / question | `obj-2 / q-2.1` | none: the step serves nothing | | owner | `sre-reliability` or a named human; decider when the step decides | "team" | | inputs | Specific evidence, documents, access, prior steps | "context" | | actions | Ordered, concrete, startable by someone else | "investigate the issue" | | outputs | Board artifacts and documents by standard and path | "notes" | | exit criterion | Observable condition that ends the step | "when done" | | redirect if | Result that changes the plan, and where it goes | missing on investigations | | verification | How someone else checks the output | "looks right" | | depends on | Step IDs | implicit ordering | | effort | Fibonacci comparative signal (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13) | hours promised as fact | | risks | What could go wrong and the mitigation | none | Keep steps small enough that the exit criterion is checkable in one sitting or one PR. Split a step whose actions serve two objectives with different owners. #### Investigation plan Use in `investigate` mode. Order by **information gain per unit cost**: cheap steps that can kill or confirm a central hypothesis come first. Every step names the hypothesis or question it discriminates and what each plausible result means. ```markdown #### Investigation plan — ### Hypotheses under test | ID | Hypothesis | Evidence for | Evidence against | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | H1 | ... | ... | ... | live | ### Steps #### inv-1 — (obj-1 / q-1.1, H1 vs H2) · owner: evidence-researcher · effort 2 - Inputs: ... - Actions: 1. ... 2. ... - Outputs: finding artifacts with evidence IDs; updated hypothesis table - Exit: - Redirect if: → skip to inv-4 / close H2 / escalate to user - Verification: - Depends on: — - Risks: ... ### Decision points - After inv-2: if , switch to `decide` mode with options A/B; otherwise continue inv-3. ### Stop conditions - Objective success measures met, or budget reached (persist and report). ``` #### Decision plan Use in `decide` mode. The plan gets to a well-formed decision record and then hands off. ```markdown #### Decision plan — - Door: one-way | two-way · Decider: · Consulted: · Informed: - Evaluation criteria (weights only if the decider sets them): ... ### Options | Option | Summary | Criteria scores with evidence | Owner of strongest case | | --- | --- | --- | --- | ### Steps #### dec-1 — Independent assessments · owners: <3–5 experts> · effort 3 - Actions: each expert assesses every option against the criteria without seeing the others; cites evidence. - Exit: one assessment per expert per option on the board. #### dec-2 — Targeted critique / sidebars - Actions: open a disagreement sidebar only where assessments conflict on facts. - Exit: every conflict harvested. #### dec-3 — Contra-memo (one-way doors only) - Owner: strongest dissenter. Output: the full case for the leading alternative. #### dec-4 — Decision record - Owner: facilitator drafts; decider accepts. Output: decision record with Y-statement, stances, confirmation check. #### dec-5 — Follow-on - Implementation or validation steps that the decision triggers, with owners. ``` #### Implementation plan Use in `implement` mode. The central artifact is the validation plan: every objective/ask maps to at least one observable check, and every step maps back to an objective. Reach a first end-to-end validated slice before breadth. ```markdown #### Implementation plan — ### Validation plan | Ask / objective | Acceptance check | Method | Layer | Runs in | Evidence when done | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | obj-2 | Denied role sees an explanation and no data | features/access.feature scenario "…" + integration test | backend, UI | PR pipeline | test IDs | planned | ### Documentation set | Document | Standard | Owner | Serves | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | features/access.feature | Gherkin | requirements-analyst | obj-2 | | docs/adr/0007-*.md | MADR + Y | solution-architect | dec-0007 | | docs/architecture/c4-container.mmd | C4 (Mermaid) | solution-architect | obj-1 | ### Steps #### impl-1 — Walking skeleton (obj-1, obj-2) · owner: · effort 5 - Inputs: ... - Actions: 1. ... - Outputs: ... - Exit: first scenario of features/access.feature passes end to end in CI - Verification: CI run link; reviewer re-runs locally - Depends on: — - Risks: ... ### Lanes and join points - Lane A (backend) impl-2, impl-3 · Lane B (UI) impl-4 · Join at impl-5: integration review against shared invariants. ### Release and rollback - Stages, proceed/hold/abort gates, rollback steps, owner. ``` When the user asks for tickets, project each step into one ticket with the same fields; don't invent work that has no step. #### Rendering rules - Lead with the mission, objective tree, and verdict; the steps follow. - Use tables for hypotheses, options, validation, and documents; use numbered actions inside steps. - Show the critical path explicitly (e.g. `inv-1 → inv-2 → dec-4 → impl-1`). - Mark steps that need human authority with the decider's name. - Keep the plan honest: unresolved questions appear as steps with exit criteria, not as hidden assumptions. #### Worked mini-example Mission: "Decide whether to move nightly batch reports to streaming." Mode `investigate → decide`. - `inv-1` (data-analyst, effort 2): measure which reports users open within an hour of generation. Exit: usage table for all 14 reports. Redirect if fewer than 2 reports are time-sensitive → recommend closing as non-goal. - `inv-2` (solution-architect, effort 3): map current pipeline as a C4 container view and list coupling points. Exit: diagram reviewed by sre-reliability. - `dec-1..4`: options "status quo", "stream the 3 time-sensitive reports", "full streaming"; finance-analyst owns cost, sre-reliability owns operability; decision record dec-0003 with Y-statement and stances. - `impl-1` (follow-on, only if streaming wins): walking skeleton for one report with a Gherkin freshness scenario.
